title: Bento Grid vs Maximalism
lede: One arranges many things calmly. The other arranges many things loudly. Both are answers to the same problem: a page that has more than five things to say.
verdict: Bento controls size — a 4-column grid, one 16px gap, tiles that span one or two columns. Maximalism controls none of that: cards are rotated by a fixed degree each, borders are 2px black, and the palette runs to five colours on purpose.
brief: Bento is a discipline about proportion. The grid is repeat(4, 1fr) with a gap that never changes, and every tile is a multiple of that unit — one column, or two. Because nothing is rotated, nothing overlaps and the gap is constant, the page reads as one object rather than a set of cards.

Maximalism in this gallery is not random. Each card carries a fixed small rotation (−1.5deg on the hero label, ±1deg on the nav chips), borders are a flat 2px #16130f, and fills come from a five-colour set: butter, mint, pink, lilac, blue. The composition holds only because the rotations are small and repeatable and the palette is capped — remove either and it reads as a broken layout rather than a busy one.

whenA: The page must show six or more capabilities without becoming a wall of cards
There is genuinely different weight in the content — one claim, three features, one number — that spans can express
The brand is quiet and the page has to stay readable for several minutes
whenB: The page is a poster, a campaign or a portfolio opening, and five seconds is the whole visit
Each item is meant to feel individually placed, not part of a system
You can cap the palette and the rotations — without those two limits it collapses into noise
promptDelta: Ask for spans and a constant gap and you get Bento; ask for fixed rotations, 2px outlines and five named fills and you get maximalism. The failure mode is a mix: a model asked for a "playful bento" will rotate some tiles, which destroys the one property that makes bento legible — the constant gap between unrotated boxes. If you want playfulness with structure, rotate the label, not the tile.
